# Margaret's Careful Distance

Margaret sits in the leather chair across from me with her hands folded in her lap, a posture that speaks of discipline and control. At seventy-six, she carries herself with the composed bearing of someone accustomed to making critical decisions under pressure. Her silver hair is perfectly arranged, her cardigan pressed. She has been a radiologist for nearly fifty years—the kind of physician who spent her career reading images others missed, spotting the small shadows that changed everything.

She begins by telling me about the summer of 1982, when she was a young woman of thirty-four, freshly divorced and searching for meaning. She had taken a three-month leave from her radiology practice in Toronto to volunteer with Doctors Without Borders in Lebanon. The civil war was accelerating. She thought her skills could help. She thought she could make a difference.

The hospital in Beirut where she worked was a converted school building with inadequate equipment and no backup power. She spent her days in a basement room reading chest X-rays and abdominal films, trying to identify injuries in images degraded by age and poor technique. Around her, the sounds of shelling grew closer. She remembers the particular vibration of nearby explosions—how they rattled through the building's bones and through her own body.

On the morning of July 14th, a direct hit struck the hospital's east wing. Margaret was reading films when the blast threw her against the wall. She lost consciousness. When she woke, she was being carried out by colleagues, her left arm hanging at an odd angle. The hospital was collapsing. Later, she would learn that twelve patients in the ward above her had died. The radiologist who had worked the morning shift before her—a woman she had shared lunch with—was among them.

Margaret returned to Canada after six weeks in a Lebanese hospital and two months of rehabilitation. She resumed her practice. She married her current husband, Robert, two years later. They had a good life. She raised two children. She built a respected career. By all accounts, she moved forward.

But Margaret has never truly left that basement room.

She tells me that for the past year, her sleep has become almost impossible. She lies awake beside Robert, her mind cycling through the same images: the X-ray light box glowing in the darkness, the moment the walls shook, the face of her colleague in the hallway that morning. When she does sleep, she dreams of images she never actually saw—radiographs of injuries too severe to survive, films that somehow contain the moment of death itself.

During the day, she has largely retired from radiology, though she still consults on difficult cases from home. She finds that she cannot tolerate the hospital environment anymore. The fluorescent lights, the hum of the equipment, the sense of enclosed spaces—they all trigger a tightness in her chest that makes breathing difficult. She has begun to avoid going out altogether. Robert does most of the shopping now. She tells me she is simply "being practical" about her age, but her voice wavers.

What troubles her most is the hypervigilance that has intensified with age. She monitors news from the Middle East obsessively, checking her phone multiple times daily for updates. She has installed new locks on the house. When she hears sirens—common enough in the city—her heart races and she finds herself mentally calculating escape routes, assessing structural vulnerabilities, preparing for impact.

Margaret describes all of this with clinical detachment, as though she is reading her own case file. But when she mentions her grandson asking why Grandma won't go to his soccer games anymore, her eyes fill with tears. She wipes them away quickly, as though they are a diagnostic error she must correct.
